title: Which Choice (Specific Goal)
intro: Choose the answer that does exactly what the question asks.

sections.heading: Answer the question that is actually asked
body: Restate the question’s goal before reading choices: emphasize danger, supply a specific detail, or conclude the paragraph.
A choice can be true and well written yet fail the goal. Check every requirement and then reread the choice in context.

examples.text: Goal: emphasize speed. 'The sprinter crossed the line in under ten seconds.'
examples.label: names the speed — meets the goal

examples.text: Goal: emphasize speed. 'The sprinter wore bright blue running shoes.'
examples.label: true but says nothing about speed

sections.tip: Restate the goal in your own words first. Then ask of each choice: does this do that exact thing?

sections.heading: Match concrete goals to concrete details
body: For a quality such as speed or danger, look for a concrete detail that demonstrates it: a number, sensory observation, or specific action.
For support or illustration, connect the detail directly to the stated claim. Being on the same general topic is not enough.

examples.text: Goal: show the cave is huge. 'The cavern could swallow a ten-story building whole.'
examples.label: a concrete image of huge size

examples.text: Goal: show the cave is huge. 'The cavern was discovered by two local teenagers.'
examples.label: on topic but says nothing about size

sections.tip: For emphasis goals, hunt for the choice with a number, a measurement, or a vivid concrete image.

sections.heading: Conclusions, introductions, and tone
body: An introduction previews what follows; a conclusion returns to the main point; a transition connects adjacent ideas. Read the surrounding sentences before choosing.
For tone, match the passage’s voice. Reject wording that becomes too casual, too formal, or more intense than the surrounding text.

examples.text: Goal: conclude a paragraph on teamwork. 'In the end, no single player won the game; the team did.'
examples.label: ties back to the teamwork point

examples.text: Goal: conclude a paragraph on teamwork. 'The stadium was built in 1962.'
examples.label: a fact that ignores the paragraph's point

sections.tip: For intro and conclusion goals, reread the neighboring sentences so you know exactly what the choice must connect to.

sections.heading: How to spot these questions
body: Look for goal phrases such as “most effectively emphasizes” or “best concludes.” Content often changes while the choices remain grammatically plausible.
State the goal, test each option against it, then read your choice in context. NO CHANGE competes on the same terms.
sections.tip: If two choices both sound good, reread the goal. Exactly one of them does the stated job, and the goal words break the tie.

sections.heading: Advanced transfer: a whole-essay goal and an earned conclusion
body: For an essay-level goal, summarize the argument or narrative arc before choosing a local revision. A conclusion may echo an opening image with a changed meaning rather than simply repeat the thesis.

Test every part of the goal: linking an image, showing a change, and maintaining tone are separate demands. An on-topic sentence can still fail because it introduces a new claim, merely summarizes facts, or overstates the change.

examples.text: Opening: a grandmother's worn quilt has a new patch in every generation. After the essay traces the family members who repaired it, the conclusion says, 'The newest stitches are mine, but the pattern still carries all of their hands.'
examples.label: The quilt image returns with a changed meaning: inherited craft continues through the writer.

examples.text: Conclusion: 'Good-quality cotton thread can be expensive, so compare prices before buying it.'
examples.label: The practical advice concerns quilting but abandons the essay’s image and family meaning.

sections.tip: State the essay’s starting image, the change it develops, and what the conclusion must make the reader understand.

sections.heading: Whole-essay purpose: test the requested goal against the whole text
body: Break the proposed goal into its required parts, then summarize what each paragraph actually contributes. A shared subject does not prove that an essay explains a mechanism, compares alternatives, or supports an argument.

Check whether the text develops those required parts across its paragraphs. One passing mention is insufficient for a sustained comparison. Judge every answer’s verdict and reason against the actual essay; missing details matter only if the specified goal requires them.

examples.text: Goal: explain how a garden’s funding changed. Paragraph 1: Membership fees paid the first year’s rent. Paragraph 2: When the rent increased, the organizers began selling seedlings. Paragraph 3: The sales now cover rent while fees buy shared tools. This essay meets the goal.
examples.label: The paragraphs trace the original source, the pressure for change and the new division of costs.

examples.text: Goal: compare two ways of preserving a mural. Paragraph 1 recounts the artist’s childhood. Paragraph 2 describes the painting of the mural. Paragraph 3 mentions that a protective coating was added, then returns to the artist’s later career. This essay does not meet the comparison goal.
examples.label: One coating is mentioned, but the text never develops two methods or their relative strengths.

check.stem: By mile twenty-five, [[the runner was still moving forward]].
check.questionText: The writer wants to emphasize the runner's exhaustion late in the race. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
choices: the crowd's cheers echoed down the tree-lined streets
the runner could see several of the city's historic landmarks
the runner's legs burned and her vision swam with every stride
the course turned north to follow the river
check.explanation: Only 'the runner's legs burned and her vision swam with every stride' shows exhaustion through physical detail; the cheering crowd, the visible landmarks, and the course turning north all describe the scene without saying anything about how tired she is.

check.stem: Crews this month are pouring the final sections of the new dam, [[a major addition to the river valley]].
check.questionText: The writer wants to emphasize the dam's enormous scale. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
choices: a structure that will rise 600 feet and stretch nearly a mile across the canyon
a project designed by a team of regional engineers
a replacement for an aging dam on the same river
a project funded largely by a local energy company
check.explanation: 'Rise 600 feet and stretch nearly a mile' gives measurements that show size directly; the engineering team, the aging dam being replaced, and the funding source are facts about the project's history and backing, not its scale.

check.stem: A paragraph describes how a community garden turned a vacant lot into a gathering place where neighbors who had never spoken now swap seeds and recipes. The writer wants to add a final sentence.
check.questionText: Which choice best concludes the paragraph by reinforcing its main idea?
choices: Tomatoes and peppers, the garden's most popular crops, need at least six hours of full sun.
The garden occupies a half-acre lot two blocks from the elementary school.
Several local businesses donated the seeds for the first planting.
What was once an empty lot is now the place where strangers become neighbors.
check.explanation: 'What was once an empty lot is now the place where strangers become neighbors' restates the paragraph's point that the garden brings people together; the crops' sunlight needs, the lot's location, and the seed donors are stray facts that reinforce nothing.
